questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: InsightLab runs a multi-agent research system: a coordinator decomposes the client's question and delegates to web search, document analysis, and synthesis subagents, which together produce reports with citations.

For the question "What is the state of the energy transition in Brazil?", the final report covered almost nothing but solar energy. The logs show that the coordinator created three subtasks: "cost of solar panels", "residential solar adoption", and "solar incentives". All the subagents did their jobs well. Where is the problem, and how should it be fixed?
opcoes: In the search subagents, which should have realized that the topic was broader and extended, on their own, the scope of the subtasks they received from the coordinator.
In the decomposition: the coordinator should decompose more broadly (wind, biofuels, grid...) and check coverage.
In the synthesis subagent, which should have filled in the gaps with its own knowledge.
In the number of subagents: doubling the number of searches on the same three topics would increase coverage.
questoes.explicacao: Overly narrow decomposition anti-pattern: competent subagents covering only part of the topic. Decompose more broadly and check coverage explicitly.
feedbacks: Tempting, but the subagents did exactly what was asked; expecting them to go beyond their scope makes the system unpredictable.
Correct. The subagents performed poorly chosen tasks well. The failure is in the decomposition, and the fix is to broaden the subtasks and verify coverage.
Filling gaps without sources compromises provenance; at most, the synthesis should flag the gap.
More searches on the same narrow topics only deepen the bias; the problem is what was decomposed, not how much.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: InsightLab runs a multi-agent research system: a coordinator decomposes the client's question and delegates to web search, document analysis, and synthesis subagents, which together produce reports with citations.

The coordinator delegates to the analysis subagent with the prompt "analyze the sources found and highlight what is relevant". The result comes back generic and sometimes analyzes the wrong documents. What is the fix?
opcoes: Have the subagent receive the coordinator's full history before starting, so it has exactly the same context as the main conversation.
Replace the analysis subagent with a more capable model.
Have the subagent ask the end user clarifying questions whenever it is in doubt.
Explicitly pass the question, the documents, the relevance criterion, and the output format in the prompt.
questoes.explicacao: The subagent's context is isolated: the question, the material, the criteria, and the output format go explicitly in the delegation prompt.
feedbacks: It dumps noise and tokens onto the subagent and cancels out the advantage of the isolated context; the right approach is to pass only what is needed, explicitly.
A better model still doesn't know which sources to analyze or for which question. It targets the wrong symptom.
It shifts the coordinator's delegation failure onto the user and breaks the automated flow.
Correct. The subagent has an isolated context and doesn't inherit the coordinator's history; everything it needs must go explicitly in the prompt.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: InsightLab runs a multi-agent research system: a coordinator decomposes the client's question and delegates to web search, document analysis, and synthesis subagents, which together produce reports with citations.

A typical research job requires five independent searches. The logs show the coordinator emitting one Agent call per turn, waiting for the result before the next one; each report takes 25 minutes. How can latency be reduced without losing quality?
opcoes: Have the coordinator emit the five Agent calls in the same response, so the subagents run in parallel.
Combine the five searches into a single subagent with a large prompt.
Reduce the research to two searches, the most important ones.
Use the Batch API for the searches, since it is cheaper.
questoes.explicacao: To parallelize, the coordinator emits multiple Agent calls in the same response. Separate turns = sequential.
feedbacks: Correct. Parallelism happens when multiple Agent calls go out in the same coordinator response; separate turns are sequential.
It goes back to being sequential within a single context, which becomes overloaded; isolation and specialization are lost.
It cuts latency by sacrificing coverage; the problem was the sequential execution, not the number of searches.
Batch has a processing window of up to 24h, with no SLA, and doesn't support each subagent's multi-turn tool loop; it would increase latency.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: InsightLab runs a multi-agent research system: a coordinator decomposes the client's question and delegates to web search, document analysis, and synthesis subagents, which together produce reports with citations.

To "speed things up", an engineer made the search subagents send results directly to the synthesis subagent, and the synthesis subagent request extra searches directly from the search subagents. Now nobody can say which sources went into the report or why some searches are repeated. Which architecture fixes this?
opcoes: A shared message bus on which all of the subagents publish and read results, with a central log to keep track of who sent what.
Keep the direct communication and add more detailed logs in each subagent.
Hub-and-spoke: all traffic goes through the coordinator, which delegates, aggregates, handles errors, and re-delegates.
Merge search and synthesis into a single agent with all the tools.
questoes.explicacao: Hub-and-spoke: the coordinator decomposes, delegates, routes all communication, aggregates, and handles errors. Subagents talking to each other directly is an anti-pattern.
feedbacks: It formalizes direct communication between subagents; it increases coupling and still lacks a single point that controls coverage and errors.
It improves observation of the chaos, not the design; subagents talking to each other directly is the anti-pattern.
Correct. The coordinator routes all communication, which provides traceability, gap control, and centralized error handling.
It eliminates the communication, but also the specialization and context isolation; the single agent becomes overloaded.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: InsightLab runs a multi-agent research system: a coordinator decomposes the client's question and delegates to web search, document analysis, and synthesis subagents, which together produce reports with citations.

Clients also ask simple questions such as "what Selic rate was set at the last Copom meeting?". Today, every question goes through search, document analysis, and synthesis, taking minutes and costing a lot. What should the coordinator do?
opcoes: Keep the full pipeline, because standardization guarantees quality.
Create a separate system, with a smaller model and a classifier at the entry point, dedicated only to simple factual questions, keeping the current pipeline for everything else.
Answer simple questions using only the model's knowledge, without searching.
Invoke only the subagents the query needs (here, one search and a short answer with a source).
questoes.explicacao: Invoke only the subagents the query needs; don't push everything through the entire pipeline.
feedbacks: Standardization here is a waste of time and money; it doesn't increase the quality of a simple factual answer.
More complex than necessary; the coordinator already exists to decide what to invoke.
It loses timeliness and source citation; a recent rate requires a search.
Correct. The coordinator invokes only what the query requires; not every question needs the entire pipeline.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: InsightLab runs a multi-agent research system: a coordinator decomposes the client's question and delegates to web search, document analysis, and synthesis subagents, which together produce reports with citations.

When it receives the results of the first round, the coordinator notices that the synthesis draft on "AI regulation in Latin America" has nothing on Chile and Colombia, which were in the requested scope. What is the best next action?
opcoes: Launch a second round of searches targeted at Chile and Colombia and redo the synthesis.
Deliver the report as is, since the countries covered are of good quality.
Redo the entire research from scratch with more subagents and a revised decomposition, ensuring that no country in scope is left out this time.
Ask the synthesis subagent to write about Chile and Colombia based on the model's general knowledge.
questoes.explicacao: The coordinator evaluates the synthesis, identifies gaps, and re-delegates a targeted second round before synthesizing.
feedbacks: Correct. Iterative refinement: run, evaluate, identify gaps, do a targeted round, and synthesize. Cheap and focused.
An incomplete delivery without even flagging the gap; it fails to meet the client's scope.
It wastes what is already good; the gap is localized and calls for a targeted round.
Unsourced content in a research system with citations; it compromises provenance.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: InsightLab runs a multi-agent research system: a coordinator decomposes the client's question and delegates to web search, document analysis, and synthesis subagents, which together produce reports with citations.

Today, when the academic search API times out, the search subagent returns "no studies found", and the report states that "there is no research on the topic". What should the subagent's response do in this case? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: Return a structured error indicating a transient failure, the query attempted, and whether it is retryable, instead of an empty result.
Keep the empty result, but add a generic note to the final report that "other studies may exist".
Return only the message "Search failed".
Include the partial results obtained before the timeout, marked as incomplete.
Abort the entire research and notify the client that the system is unavailable.
questoes.explicacao: Empty ≠ failure. A timeout produces a structured error (category, query attempted, retryable) and, when available, partial results marked as such; never an empty list as success.
feedbacks: Correct. A timeout means the search didn't run; the structured error lets the coordinator decide between retrying, using an alternative, or recording the gap.
It still treats a failure as 'nothing found' (silent suppression) and hides the diagnosis.
Generic error: without a category, the query attempted, or an indication of retry, the coordinator doesn't know what to do.
Correct. A partial result with an indication that it is incomplete allows the work to continue without pretending to have full coverage.
Aborting the workflow because of a failure in one source; the right move is to proceed with the partial results and note the gap.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: InsightLab runs a multi-agent research system: a coordinator decomposes the client's question and delegates to web search, document analysis, and synthesis subagents, which together produce reports with citations.

Of the four search subagents in a research job, three finished successfully and one failed with a permission error: the patent database requires a credential that has expired. What is the coordinator's best response?
opcoes: Retry the patent search with exponential backoff until it works.
Synthesize with the three results, record the gap (patents, and why), and flag the expired credential.
Abort the entire research job, since the report would be incomplete.
Proceed with the three results and omit the patent database from the report, since the client didn't explicitly ask for patents and the gap could raise questions.
questoes.explicacao: Don't abort the workflow because of one step: continue with the partial results, note the gap, and offer an alternative or escalate. A permission error is non-retryable.
feedbacks: Retrying only helps with transient errors; an expired credential won't come back on its own.
Correct. A permission error is not retryable; continue with the partial results, note the gap, and escalate what requires human action.
It throws away three good results because of one source; the anti-pattern of aborting the workflow over one failure.
Silent suppression: the client thinks patents were considered.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: InsightLab runs a multi-agent research system: a coordinator decomposes the client's question and delegates to web search, document analysis, and synthesis subagents, which together produce reports with citations.

The search subagent hits rate limits (HTTP 429) on the news API a few times per research job. Today it passes each 429 on to the coordinator, which interrupts its planning to deal with it. How should responsibility be divided?
opcoes: The coordinator centralizes the handling of all errors, including each 429, to maintain full control and a complete view of the system's state.
The subagent ignores the 429 and returns whatever it has, without notice.
The subagent retries with backoff (respecting retry-after) and only propagates what it couldn't resolve, with context.
The subagent repeats the call immediately, without waiting, until it succeeds.
questoes.explicacao: The subagent recovers from transient errors locally (backoff) and propagates only what it couldn't resolve, with context on what was attempted.
feedbacks: It overloads the coordinator with operational details that the subagent can resolve on its own, and it pollutes the coordinator's context.
Silent suppression: the incomplete coverage doesn't show up anywhere.
Correct. Local recovery from transient errors in the subagent; the coordinator receives only persistent failures, together with what was attempted.
Retrying without backoff aggravates the rate limit and may never converge.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: InsightLab runs a multi-agent research system: a coordinator decomposes the client's question and delegates to web search, document analysis, and synthesis subagents, which together produce reports with citations.

Two market reports, both from 2025, estimate the Brazilian fintech market at R$ 42 billion and R$ 51 billion, using different methodologies. How should the synthesis subagent handle this in the report?
opcoes: Present both values, each with its source, date, and methodology, marking the data point as contested.
Use the average, R$ 46.5 billion, as a consensus estimate.
Use the value from the better-known source and omit the other.
Omit the market size from the report, since the sources disagree.
questoes.explicacao: Conflict between sources: annotate the divergent values with their sources. Don't silently pick one or take an average.
feedbacks: Correct. A conflict between sources is annotated with the divergent values and their sources; the reader decides with complete information.
Averaging creates a number that no source states and hides the divergence.
Silently picking one value eliminates relevant information and the real uncertainty.
It throws away useful information; the divergence itself is a finding that should be presented.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: InsightLab runs a multi-agent research system: a coordinator decomposes the client's question and delegates to web search, document analysis, and synthesis subagents, which together produce reports with citations.

The consistency checker flagged a "contradiction" because one source says 38% of SMEs use the cloud and another says 61%. The first is a survey published in 2021 with 2020 data; the second, from 2025 with 2024 data. Which design avoids this false alarm?
opcoes: Automatically discard sources more than three years old.
Keep only the most recent source when two numbers diverge, since newer data better reflects the current state of the market.
Ask the checker to "use good judgment" when comparing numbers.
Record the data period and the publication date, treating different periods as a series, not a contradiction.
questoes.explicacao: Record the data period, the publication date, and the collection date. Numbers from different periods are not a contradiction.
feedbacks: It loses useful history (the evolution from 38% to 61% is a finding) and doesn't solve the metadata problem.
It picks silently; and, when the sources are from the same period, it would erase a real conflict.
A vague criterion; without the data date in the metadata, the checker has no way of knowing.
Correct. Temporal data requires recording 'data as of', publication, and collection; values from different periods describe an evolution.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: InsightLab runs a multi-agent research system: a coordinator decomposes the client's question and delegates to web search, document analysis, and synthesis subagents, which together produce reports with citations.

The analysis subagents return paragraphs of running text. In the final synthesis, several claims lose their source, and the reviewer cannot trace where each number came from. Which change solves this at the source?
opcoes: Ask the synthesis subagent to "not lose the citations".
Structured output from the subagents separating content from metadata: claim, excerpt, source/URL, and date.
Put all the URLs consulted in a reference list at the end of the report.
Have the synthesis subagent redo the searches to find the sources of each claim again.
questoes.explicacao: Structured handoff between agents: separate content from metadata (claim, evidence, source, date) so that attribution survives.
feedbacks: A vague instruction about an input that already arrives without structure; the source is lost before the synthesis.
Correct. A structured handoff with metadata lets attribution survive the subsequent stages of the pipeline.
A loose list doesn't say which claim comes from which source; the claim → source mapping is still missing.
Expensive and fragile; it recovers after the fact what simply shouldn't have been lost.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: InsightLab runs a multi-agent research system: a coordinator decomposes the client's question and delegates to web search, document analysis, and synthesis subagents, which together produce reports with citations.

InsightLab is going to revise the synthesis subagent's instructions to improve the reliability of the reports. Which TWO practices should be included? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: Remove caveats and limitations from the sources, so the text is more assertive.
Label the degree of certainty of each finding: well-established (multiple sources), contested, or single source.
When sources diverge, present only the most conservative value.
Cite sources only in a general bibliography at the end, without linking claims to sources.
Choose the format according to the content: a table for comparable financial data, a timeline for events.
questoes.explicacao: Reliable synthesis: label certainty (well-established/contested/single source), preserve caveats, link each claim to its source, and choose the format based on the content.
feedbacks: Losing caveats distorts the evidence; they should be preserved.
Correct. The certainty label shows the reader how solid each finding is.
Silently picking a value, even a 'conservative' one, hides the conflict.
Without the claim → source mapping, provenance is lost.
Correct. A format suited to the content is part of a good synthesis.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: InsightLab runs a multi-agent research system: a coordinator decomposes the client's question and delegates to web search, document analysis, and synthesis subagents, which together produce reports with citations.

The search subagent has two tools: search ("searches for information") and find_documents ("finds relevant documents"). The first queries the web; the second, the internal collection of licensed reports. The subagent frequently searches the web for what exists in the collection. What is the simplest and most effective fix?
opcoes: Add a classifier in front of the subagent that analyzes each query and decides which of the two tools should be used before the model acts.
Remove web search, leaving only the internal collection.
Rename the tools and rewrite their descriptions (e.g., web_search and search_licensed_reports), stating when to use each one.
Force the subagent to always call both tools for every query.
questoes.explicacao: Vague, overlapping descriptions cause misrouting: rename and describe the tools to separate their purposes.
feedbacks: More complex than necessary; differentiating the descriptions comes first.
It eliminates a capability needed for topics outside the collection.
Correct. The name and description are the selection criterion; tools whose descriptions overlap in purpose cause misrouting.
It doubles cost and latency and dumps redundant results into the context, instead of fixing the selection.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: InsightLab runs a multi-agent research system: a coordinator decomposes the client's question and delegates to web search, document analysis, and synthesis subagents, which together produce reports with citations.

The synthesis subagent receives, in a single prompt, the raw results from 12 subagents (about 150,000 tokens). Important findings that appear in the middle of this material almost never make it into the report. What should be done?
opcoes: Each subagent returns a concise summary (key findings first, with source), organized under topic headings.
Use a model with a 1M-token window, so the 150,000 tokens fit comfortably and the model has room to consider all the results.
Repeat the 150,000 tokens twice in the prompt to reinforce attention.
Shuffle the order of the results on each run so that every finding has a chance of being at the beginning.
questoes.explicacao: Lost in the middle: key findings at the beginning, section headings, nothing critical in the middle; and cut the volume with concise outputs.
feedbacks: Correct. Lost in the middle: put key findings at the beginning, use headings, and reduce the volume with concise, structured outputs.
Fitting is not the problem; a larger window costs more, and the 'lost in the middle' effect persists or gets worse.
It doubles cost and noise without solving how the material is organized.
It makes the result random and non-reproducible; it doesn't fix the cause.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: InsightLab runs a multi-agent research system: a coordinator decomposes the client's question and delegates to web search, document analysis, and synthesis subagents, which together produce reports with citations.

Large research jobs run for hours. When the coordinator process crashes in the third hour, everything restarts from scratch, including the searches that had already finished. Which design solves this?
opcoes: Resume the coordinator with --resume in the same session, relying on the conversation history to know which searches had already finished before the crash.
Reduce the scope of the research jobs so they finish in under an hour.
Add a time limit per research job and mark those that exceed it as failed.
Keep a manifest in a known location (subtasks, status, result paths) and resume from it.
questoes.explicacao: State saved in a known location + a coordinator manifest makes it possible to resume after a crash. Whatever cannot be lost goes to a file.
feedbacks: It depends on the scrollback, which may have been compacted or lost; whatever cannot be lost goes to a file.
It sacrifices the product to work around an engineering flaw.
It doesn't recover anything; it only turns crashes into declared failures.
Correct. State saved to a file + a manifest makes it possible to resume after a crash without redoing what has already finished.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: InsightLab runs a multi-agent research system: a coordinator decomposes the client's question and delegates to web search, document analysis, and synthesis subagents, which together produce reports with citations.

The system is implemented with the Claude Agent SDK, and the subagents are declared via AgentDefinition. Which TWO statements about this implementation are correct? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: Each subagent automatically receives the coordinator's full history.
Subagents can directly call sibling subagents to exchange results.
The coordinator must have the Agent tool in allowedTools to be able to create subagents.
Messages produced inside a subagent carry parent_tool_use_id, which allows them to be attributed to the call that created it.
To run in parallel, each subagent must be started in a separate SDK process.
questoes.explicacao: Agent SDK: the Agent tool must be in allowedTools; subagent messages carry parent_tool_use_id. Context is isolated, and communication goes through the coordinator.
feedbacks: False: the subagent's context is isolated, and everything it needs goes in the prompt.
It contradicts hub-and-spoke: communication goes through the coordinator.
Correct. Subagents are created via the Agent tool (formerly called Task), which must be allowed for the coordinator.
Correct. This is how you trace which subagent produced what.
Parallelism comes from multiple Agent calls in the same coordinator response.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: InsightLab runs a multi-agent research system: a coordinator decomposes the client's question and delegates to web search, document analysis, and synthesis subagents, which together produce reports with citations.

The analysis subagent's prompt says "discard unreliable sources". In different runs, the same technical blog is accepted in one and discarded in another, and studies from industry associations are treated inconsistently. What is the best fix?
opcoes: Ask the subagent to assign each source a reliability score from 0 to 10, justifying the score, and automatically discard those below 7.
Add "be rigorous" to the current instruction.
Define explicit criteria: the source types that count, those that don't, and boundary examples with the reason.
Add a second subagent that reviews each decision of the first one using the same prompt.
questoes.explicacao: Explicit criteria (what counts, what doesn't, boundary examples) beat vague instructions like 'discard unreliable sources'.
feedbacks: It shifts the vague judgment to a self-reported score with no yardstick; it remains inconsistent.
Yet another vague instruction; it doesn't define rigor.
Correct. Explicit criteria, with what counts, what doesn't, and boundary cases, make the decision consistent.
It doubles the cost and replicates the same vague criterion; it doesn't solve the root cause.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: InsightLab runs a multi-agent research system: a coordinator decomposes the client's question and delegates to web search, document analysis, and synthesis subagents, which together produce reports with citations.

The search subagent uses the server-side web search tool. In extensive research, the response sometimes comes back with stop_reason "pause_turn", and the current code treats this as the end, delivering an incomplete result. What is the correct handling?
opcoes: Treat pause_turn as an error and repeat the original request from scratch.
Resend the conversation including the response received, so the model continues the server-side loop where it left off.
Increase max_tokens, since pause_turn indicates that the output was cut off.
Switch to tool_choice none on the next turn to force a final answer.
questoes.explicacao: pause_turn = the server-side tool loop hit its iteration cap; resend the response to continue.
feedbacks: It discards the work already done in the turn and may hit the same cap again.
Correct. pause_turn indicates that the server-side loop hit its iteration cap; resending the response allows it to continue.
It confuses pause_turn with max_tokens; they are different signals.
It forces an answer before the search finishes; it delivers exactly the incomplete result you want to avoid.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: InsightLab runs a multi-agent research system: a coordinator decomposes the client's question and delegates to web search, document analysis, and synthesis subagents, which together produce reports with citations.

To reduce incorrect citations, the team asked the synthesis subagent, when it finishes the report, to "review its own citations". The rate of citations that don't support the claim barely changed. Which approach is better?
opcoes: An independent verifier subagent, with a fresh context, that checks whether each cited excerpt supports the claim.
Ask the synthesis subagent to review the citations twice.
Ask the synthesis subagent for a confidence score for each citation, with a justification, and remove from the report the citations scored below the threshold.
Increase the synthesis subagent's effort.
questoes.explicacao: Review should be done by an independent instance (without the author's reasoning context), with explicit criteria.
feedbacks: Correct. Self-review in the same context suffers from the bias of the reasoning that generated the text; an independent verifier, with explicit criteria, catches what the author rationalized.
Same session, same bias; repeating doesn't change the point of view.
Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated; incorrect citations usually come with high confidence.
More reasoning in the same biased context doesn't fix self-review.
